variables.name: fed_pip
variables.description: Bree fed Pip sardines from the galley larder, so he purrs.

variables.name: knows_ropes
variables.description: Bree crossed the rope-bridge low and slow, so she has climbed live rope.

variables.name: told_bosun
variables.description: Bree told the bosun the truth, that she is a stowaway.

variables.name: fin_free
variables.description: Bree untangled the harness strap from the fin of Nimbus.

nodes.body: A girl named Bree had dreamed about the sky for as long as she could remember, and now she was flying in it. The great airship Cirrus had just cast off from the mooring tower, with ropes creaking and steam hissing past the rail. "Cast off, and smartly now!" called a dry, quick voice from the bridge, and that was Captain Quill. Bree could not see her, because Bree could not see much of anything. She was curled up small inside a coil of rope on the boarding deck, a real stowaway at last. Heavy boots thumped past her hiding place, and nobody looked down.

choices.label: Slip out of the rope coil.

nodes.body: Bree uncurled and peeked over the top of the coil. Four ways led off the boarding deck. A hatch in the floor rumbled and breathed out hot air from the engine room below. A ramp sloped down into the dark cargo hold, where rows of crates disappeared into shadow. A ladder climbed the mast toward the crow's nest and the open sky. And a pair of glass doors glowed gold, with music and laughter spilling out of the grand saloon. "You there, coil that line!" a sailor shouted, and although he was not shouting at Bree, he was walking her way.

choices.label: Slip down the hatch to the engine room.
Creep down the ramp into the cargo hold.
Climb the ladder toward the crow's nest.
Sneak through the glass doors into the grand saloon.

nodes.body: The engine room roared with noise, and the air smelled of hot oil. Brass pistons pumped up and down without ever slowing. A big stoker stood with his back to her, shoveling coal into the fire and singing to the engine as he worked. "Eat up, old girl, because we have a long night ahead," he rumbled. Above him ran a narrow catwalk, and when Bree tested the rail with her hand, it felt sturdy. The catwalk led the long way round, to a quiet corner where pipes glowed orange in the gloom. The open floor was quicker, but it ran right behind the stoker's boots.

choices.label: Creep along the catwalk.
Dart across the open floor.

nodes.body: Past the pistons, the pipes closed in like a warm brass forest, and the scrape of the stoker's shovel faded behind her. On one wall, a row of dials ticked and trembled, each with a small brass label. Bree read the nearest ones, which said STEAM and LIFT, and then one that said only HOLD. Beside the dials, a short ladder dropped into the coal bunkers. Something was scuffling about down there in the dark, something too small to be a sailor and too bold to be a mouse. It scuffled, stopped, and scuffled again.

choices.label: Study the ticking dials.
Climb down toward the scuffling.

nodes.body: The dials were easy to read, once Bree had studied them for a while. STEAM showed how hard the boilers were pushing, and LIFT showed how well the great balloon held the ship up. Fire was turning into flight, right there on the wall. But the dial marked HOLD made no sense at all, because its needle pointed at a word instead of a number, and the word was WARM. Somebody had chalked a note beneath it: keep it WARM down there, by order of the captain. Why would cargo need to be kept warm? Past the dials, a low hatch stood open a crack, and warm air sighed through the gap.

choices.label: Duck through the low hatch.

nodes.body: Through the hatch ran a snug passage, lit by oil lamps that swung gently on their hooks. The roar of the engine sank to a friendly rumble, and then Bree heard a new sound. It was a small mew, somewhere ahead, and it did not sound scared so much as curious. Bree whispered a hello into the dimness. The mew came again, a little closer, and this time it sounded like an answer. She followed it along the passage, from one pool of lamplight to the next.

choices.label: Follow the mewing along the passage.

nodes.body: Bree climbed down the ladder toward the scuffling, into coal bunkers that were hot and dim. The scuffling stopped at once. In the black dust at her feet, she found a line of tiny paw prints, which went around a coal heap, over a shovel, and straight to a loose hatch that swung on its hinge. "So you are not a mouse after all," Bree whispered. A sound drifted back through the hatch, half mew and half chirp. It did not sound like trouble, but like something that wanted very much to be found.

choices.label: Squeeze through the loose hatch.

nodes.body: Beyond the hatch, a service passage ran warm along the side of the engine. The paw prints went on ahead, sooty and neat, as if somebody small had an important place to be. The roar of the pistons faded behind her, and the mew came again, closer now. Bree walked faster. The prints grew fainter as the soot wore off, until they stopped altogether at the edge of the lamplight.

choices.label: Follow the paw prints to the end.

nodes.body: The passage ended in a nook stacked with spare rope and folded canvas, far from the noise of the engine. The mew came from behind a crate marked SAILCLOTH. Bree crouched down as slowly as she could. A pair of eyes caught the lamplight and blinked at her, bright and curious, and not one bit scared.

choices.label: Kneel and look behind the crate.

nodes.body: Bree darted across the open floor, with her boots light on the metal grating. Halfway over, the stoker's song stopped and his shovel scraped to a halt. "Somebody is in my engine room," he rumbled, and his big shoulders began to turn. Bree had about one second left. To her left stood the coal chute, with a pool of black shadow behind it. To her right sat an empty coal bucket, the kind that ship's boys carried on their errands.

choices.label: Dive behind the coal chute.
Grab the coal bucket and look busy.

nodes.body: Bree dove behind the coal chute and held her breath until her chest ached. The stoker frowned at the empty floor for a long moment. "Tricks of the light," he muttered, "or tricks of the coal dust, and you saw nothing either, old girl." He patted the boiler as if it were a horse, and then his shovel began to scrape again, as steady as ever. Bree let her breath out slowly. She slipped away on her toes, deeper into the humming maze of pipes.

choices.label: Slip on into the pipe maze.

nodes.body: Bree grabbed the coal bucket and marched past the stoker as if she owned the place. He watched her go by with great interest. "That was a nice try," he said, "but that is the ash bucket, and you are carrying it upside down." He was not unkind about it, and he walked her up to the purser's office, where a thin man frowned over a ledger. "No ticket, no cabin, and no name in my book," said the purser, "which makes you cargo, miss." Bree sat on his hard little bench until the next mooring tower. But the bench had a secret, because now and then a long, low note hummed up through the wood, too sad to be an engine. "You heard nothing," said the purser. Bree had heard it three times, and she counted two more before the tower came in sight.

The cargo hold was a cave of lashed crates, where lanterns swung from the beams and the ropes creaked with every roll of the ship. Somewhere above, a deckhand was counting aloud. "Forty sacks of feed, as if we were feeding a circus," he grumbled, before his voice faded away. Two ways opened in front of Bree. One was a tidy aisle between rows of labeled boxes. The other was a gap where a cargo net had come loose and hung open like a doorway into the dark. A lantern swung toward her, and its light slid across the floor.

choices.label: Follow the tidy aisle of crates.
Wriggle through the loose netting.

nodes.body: The aisle ran deep into the hold, past row after row of silent crates. One stack was stamped with a strange crest in silver paint. Under the crest, somebody had stenciled a single word, but Bree was too far away to read it. Beside the stack, a row of barrels lay on their sides to make a low tunnel, which curved away toward the warm middle of the ship. A tuft of grey fur was caught on the rim of the first barrel.

choices.label: Read the crest on the crates.
Crawl through the barrel tunnel.

nodes.body: Up close, the crest showed a silver fish leaping over three curling clouds. But it was not really a fish, because no fish ever had fins as wide as sails. Bree read the stenciled word beneath it, which was HAVEN, and under that, in smaller letters, FEED, 40 SACKS. She poked one of the sacks through the slats of the crate, and it smelled like the sea. "Who eats forty sacks of anything?" she whispered, but nobody answered. Past the crates, a narrow gap opened in the stacked cargo, leading toward the heart of the ship.

choices.label: Slip through the gap in the cargo.

nodes.body: The gap became a walkway, squeezed between towers of freight, with one lantern swaying overhead. Ahead in the dimness, something small crossed the path, low and quick. Bree stood still, and the small thing stood still too. Then it made a sound, half mew and half chirp, and slipped behind a crate at the end of the walkway. It did not run far, and it seemed to want her to follow.

choices.label: Follow the small shape down the walkway.

nodes.body: Bree crawled into the barrel tunnel on her hands and knees. It was snug and dim, and it creaked with every sway of the ship. Halfway along, her hand landed on something soft. It turned out to be a nest of old rags, with an empty sardine tin licked perfectly clean. "Somebody lives here, and somebody small," Bree said to the dark. She crawled on and came out the far end, into a warmer part of the hold, where a narrow walkway led onward.

choices.label: Take the walkway onward.

nodes.body: The walkway was lit by one swinging lantern, and the roar of the engines grew softer with every step. Then Bree heard a small sound, half mew and half chirp, somewhere ahead of her. It came again, and again, always a little farther on. It was leading her. She followed it toward the middle of the ship, stepping over a second sardine tin on the way.

choices.label: Follow the hopeful little sound.

nodes.body: The walkway ended in a nook near the heart of the ship, where coiled rope and spare canvas were piled up, soft in the lamplight. Nothing moved, so Bree knelt down and waited. Then, behind the nearest crate, two bright eyes opened and looked straight at her. They blinked once, slowly, the way a friend might nod hello.

choices.label: Peek behind the crate.

nodes.body: Bree wriggled through the loose netting and dropped into a tangle of crates. They had come unlashed, and they shifted and groaned as the ship rolled. Then a whole wall of cargo leaned toward her, and the timbers creaked. Behind her lay the open aisle, six steps away across the sliding floor. Beside her was a narrow gap between two big boxes, just her size. The wall of crates leaned a little more.

choices.label: Scramble clear of the leaning crates.
Squeeze into the gap and wait.

nodes.body: Bree scrambled clear just as the crates settled back with a heavy groan. Dust sifted down around her. She put out a hand and steadied the nearest box until it stopped rocking. "Stay," she told it, as if it were a dog, and the box stayed. Then Bree picked her way back to the tidy aisle, where the cargo was lashed down tight, and took the safer way deeper into the hold.

choices.label: Take the safer way deeper in.

nodes.body: Bree squeezed into the gap, and the crates slid shut behind her like a door. She was not hurt, and she was not even squashed, but she was boxed into a snug wooden corner with no way out. She waited a long, dusty while. Then two bright eyes appeared at a crack that no girl could fit through, and a thin grey cat looked in at her, gave one short mrrp, and trotted away. Minutes later, a deckhand came stamping down the aisle. "All right, all right, I am coming, you noisy ghost," he grumbled, and he lifted the crates aside and stared. "Six weeks I have chased that cat without catching it once, and tonight it fetches me a girl." The purser saw Bree ashore at the next port. She looked back at the Cirrus the whole way down the tower. Somewhere aboard was a cat who had rescued her, and she did not even know his name.

The ladder to the crow's nest climbed through cold, whistling air. Far below, the deck tilted gently, and clouds slid past like slow white ships. Partway up, the ladder split in two. A sheltered inner ladder wound up inside the mast, out of the wind. Beside it, a run of open rungs went straight up the outside, where every gust could reach, with a safety line running alongside and a clip swinging loose on its end. High above, somebody was whistling a tune.

choices.label: Climb the sheltered inner ladder.
Climb the open rungs outside the mast.

nodes.body: The inner ladder ended on a small round platform, just under the floor of the crow's nest. Through the gaps in the boards above, Bree could see two big boots. The lookout was up there, whistling, with no idea that she was under his feet. A spare spyglass hung on a hook beside her. Next to it, a thick rope ran down through a hole in the platform, under a sign that said RUN, HOLD TIGHT. The boots shuffled, and the whistling stopped, and then it started up again.

choices.label: Study the balloon through the spyglass.
Slide down the rope run.

nodes.body: Through the spyglass, the great balloon became a silver sky of ribs and seams. Bree followed one seam with the glass and worked out how it all held together. Inside that skin hung the gasbags, and the gasbags held the whole ship up on nothing but air. Near the stern, though, one seam looked different, puckered and dark, like a mend on an old sock. "That one is tired," Bree whispered. She hung the spyglass back on its hook and climbed down a rigging line, toward the warmer decks below.

choices.label: Climb down the rigging line.

nodes.body: The rigging line came down in a sheltered gangway, out of the wind, where the roar of the open sky faded to a hush. Lanterns glowed along the passage. From somewhere below came a small sound, half mew and half chirp, and when it came again, it seemed to be asking her something. Bree tilted her head to listen. Then she followed the sound down a short stair, toward the middle of the ship.

choices.label: Follow the curious sound down.

nodes.body: Bree wrapped her arms and legs around the rope and slid. The run dropped her down through the mast, out of the biting wind, faster than any ladder. She landed with a soft thump on a thick coil of canvas. Above her, very faintly, the lookout was calling down the mast. "Ahoy, is somebody on my rope?" Bree grinned and kept quiet. A warm passage opened ahead of her, humming with far-off engines, and after the cold of the mast, the warmth felt like a hug.

choices.label: Take the warm inner passage.

nodes.body: The passage was snug and lit by lamps, and already the wind felt like something that had happened to somebody else. Then a small mew echoed along the corridor, faint but clear. Bree stopped to listen. The mew came again, and it sounded hopeful. She walked toward it, on toward the middle of the ship, while the mew kept just ahead of her like a guide with a very small lantern.

choices.label: Follow the mewing toward the middle.

nodes.body: Around the last corner, Bree found a nook of coiled rope and folded sail. The sound came from behind a crate, soft and clear. Bree knelt down, and two shining eyes looked back at her from the shadow. They were patient eyes, and they seemed to be waiting to see what kind of person she was.

choices.label: Look behind the crate.

nodes.body: Out on the open rungs, the wind snatched at Bree's coat, and the whole mast swayed under her hands. She was halfway up when a gust hit the ship, hard enough to make the rung under her foot shudder. The safety clip swung past her elbow, just out of reach. Above her, the rail of the crow's nest was only ten rungs away. Out over the clouds, the next gust was already coming, and it was bending the flags as it came.

choices.label: Catch the safety clip and hold on.
Scramble up before the next gust.

nodes.body: Bree caught the safety clip and snapped it onto her belt, just in time. The gust punched past a moment later and tore at her coat, but it could not tear her off the mast. She hung on with white knuckles until the air went still. "Thank you, clip," she said, quite seriously. Then she climbed back down to where the ladders split and took the sheltered inner ladder instead, glad of its solid walls at her back.

choices.label: Climb the sheltered ladder instead.

nodes.body: Bree scrambled up three more rungs before the gust caught her, and after that she could only cling and shout. "Girl ho, off the starboard mast!" bellowed a voice above. Two big hands hauled her over the rail of the crow's nest, and the lookout wrapped her in his own thick coat and gave her his cocoa. "Thirty years aloft, and I never logged one of those," he said. He kept her warm until the Cirrus reached port, talking the whole time, the way lonely lookouts do. "It is a funny thing, but she is flying heavy this trip, heavy in the belly, as if we had a whale aboard," he told her, and he laughed at his own joke. Bree was put down at port with a wave, still wondering what a ship might carry that weighed as much as a whale.

The grand saloon glowed with polished brass and soft velvet, and the passengers laughed over their supper as if nothing could ever go wrong. A steward glided between the tables with a silver tray. "More soup, madam? The chef will be so pleased," he murmured. Nobody had noticed Bree yet. Along one wall hung heavy curtains, deep with shadow. Closer by, long tablecloths hung almost to the floor, with a dark tunnel underneath them. A waiter's trolley rolled past, with its wheels clicking on the polished wood.

choices.label: Edge along the curtained wall.
Crawl under the long tablecloths.

nodes.body: Behind the curtains was a small service room, tucked out of sight. A glass case stood against the wall, full of tiny model ships. Each one was carved and painted with care, and the biggest was the Cirrus herself. Beside the case, a plain door swung on its hinge, with a card that said STEWARDS ONLY. The smell of fresh bread drifted through the gap. Out in the saloon, the steward's voice was coming closer, promising somebody the salt at once.

choices.label: Peer into the case of model ships.
Slip through the stewards' door.

nodes.body: Bree pressed her nose to the glass case, where the model of the Cirrus was cut open down the middle, like a picture in a book. Every deck was marked with a tiny label, such as BRIDGE, GALLEY, and SALOON. But the lowest deck had no label at all, because somebody had painted over it, thick and grey, as if it were not there. "Why would anybody hide a deck?" Bree whispered to the little ship. The little ship kept its secret. She slipped through the stewards' door and down the hallway beyond.

choices.label: Follow the stewards' hallway.

nodes.body: The hallway left the music and laughter behind, and it grew plainer and warmer the farther Bree walked. Lanterns hung low along the walls. Then a small sound drifted to her, half mew and half chirp, from somewhere near the middle of the ship. Bree stopped to listen. The sound came again, and it was as hard to ignore as a small paw tapping at a door, so she followed it.

choices.label: Follow the hopeful sound inward.

nodes.body: Bree slipped through the stewards' door into a narrow pantry passage, where trays of bread and cheese were stacked along one wall. She took one small crust and ate it in three bites, and it was the best crust of her life. From the saloon came the voice of the steward, as calm as cream. "A mouse, madam, on the Cirrus? I should think not," he said. Bree swallowed and tiptoed on, down a plain corridor that led away from the music.

choices.label: Follow the plain corridor onward.

nodes.body: The corridor turned snug and dim, warmed by the engines far below. A small mew drifted along it, and Bree licked the last crumb from her thumb and listened. The mew came again. It was not a frightened sound, but the sound of somebody who had smelled bread and wished to discuss it. Bree followed it deeper into the ship, toward the middle, where the lamps burned low.

choices.label: Follow the mewing toward the middle.

nodes.body: The corridor opened into a quiet nook of coiled rope and folded sailcloth. The little sound came once more, from right behind the nearest crate. Bree crouched and looked around the corner of it, and two bright eyes shone back at her. They were hopeful eyes, and patient, and not one bit afraid.

choices.label: Look gently behind the crate.

nodes.body: Bree crawled under the long tablecloths, into a forest of shoes. There were shiny shoes and buckled shoes, and one pair of slippers shaped like ducks. She was almost at the far end when a waiter's boot swung straight at her nose, because he was stepping in to pour the wine. On her left, the serving trolley had stopped, with a deep shadow under it. On her right, six steps of open floor led to a door. The boot came down an inch from her fingers.

choices.label: Roll behind the serving trolley.
Bolt across the floor for the door.

nodes.body: Bree rolled behind the serving trolley just as the waiter stepped back. She was close enough to smell the soup on his tray, which was pea soup, and it smelled wonderful. She held still until his boots clicked away. Then she slipped out the other side and tiptoed to the heavy curtains along the wall, where she found a gap, and behind the gap, a room.

choices.label: Slip behind the curtains.

nodes.body: Bree bolted for the door, in full view of the whole saloon. A lady shrieked, and a gentleman dropped his spoon in his soup. The steward caught Bree by the sleeve before she had gone four steps. He was more amused than angry. "In this saloon, miss, we walk," he said. He sat her down in the purser's office with a warm bun and a glass of milk, while the Cirrus flew steadily on. "Eat up, because you are not the oddest thing aboard this trip, not by a long way," he added, but he would not say what he meant. At the next port he saw her safely ashore, with a second bun for the road and a great deal to wonder about.

A small grey cat stepped out from behind the crate. He was thin, with ribs like the rungs of a ladder, and he had clearly been living on scraps for a long time. "Mrrp," he said, looking Bree up and down, and then he pressed his head into her hand, as if he had been waiting all voyage for someone her size. "Pip," Bree whispered, "because you look exactly like a Pip." So that was settled, and Pip, the thinnest cat in the sky, had a friend. Three ways led out of the nook. From the first came the smell of stew, and Pip's nose swung toward the galley like a compass needle. At the end of the second stood a polished door with a brass plate that said CAPTAIN. The third was a rope ladder, climbing into the inner rigging, where lanterns swayed among the ropes. Somewhere close by, a bell rang, and heavy boots began to move.

choices.label: Sneak to the galley to find Pip some food.
Creep to the captain's cabin door.
Climb the rope ladder into the rigging.

nodes.body: The galley was hot and bright, and it smelled wonderfully of stew. An enormous cook stood at the stove with his back to the door, stirring a pot the size of a bathtub and grumbling to his spoon. "Forty buckets of fish mash every day, and all of it for cargo," he muttered. "Cargo does not eat, I told her, and the captain only said, cook the mash." Pip's nose twitched. Three steps behind the cook, the larder door stood wide open, and there was cheese on the shelf. Nearer to Bree, a wall of flour sacks made a fine place to hide until he left the room. Pip's stomach growled like a very small bear.

choices.label: Creep to the open larder.
Wait behind the flour sacks.

nodes.body: Bree crept to the open larder with Pip at her heels. It was a treasure cave of bread and cheese, with a blue tin of sardines on the lowest shelf. She broke off a heel of cheese for herself and opened the sardines for Pip. He ate all six, licked the tin, and then licked it again, just in case. Then he did something he had not done before, and purred. It was a rusty, rumbling purr, like a tiny engine starting up after a long rest. "You are welcome," whispered Bree. That was when the floor lurched under them, and the hanging lamps swung hard on their chains.

choices.label: Back out of the larder.

nodes.body: Bree waited behind the flour sacks, as still as a sack herself, while the cook went on stirring and grumbling. Flour dust hung in the air like fog, and Pip's nose began to twitch. "Do not even think about it," Bree breathed, but Pip thought about it, and then he sneezed, a sneeze far too big for such a small cat. The grumbling stopped, and so did the spoon. "I know that sneeze was not mine," said the cook. The door was four steps away, the flour sacks were large, and the shadows behind them were dark. The cook's big shoes began to turn.

choices.label: Scoop up Pip and run for the door.
Hold still behind the sacks.

nodes.body: Out in the corridor, the floor tipped like a seesaw, and loose tins rolled past Bree's feet and rattled away downhill. Somewhere above, a bell began to clang, again and again, and it was certainly not a supper bell. Bree tucked Pip inside her coat, where he fit as if the coat had been made for two. "Hold on tight," she told him. Then she ran toward the noise, with the lanterns swinging wildly over her head.

choices.label: Hurry toward the clanging bell.

nodes.body: Bree held still behind the sacks, and so did Pip. The cook's big shoes came around the corner anyway. "Well, now, a girl," he said, and then he pointed his spoon at Pip, "and YOU, my sardine thief, when for six weeks I have been blaming the mate." He was far more surprised than angry. "Nobody goes hungry in my galley, not even burglars," he declared, and he fed them both a bowl of stew, and Pip had seconds. Then he marched Bree to the purser's office, grumbling all the way. "First it is forty buckets a day for the captain's cargo, and now it is cats, and what will it be next, a whale?" He laughed at that. Pip was kept on as the galley cat, since mousers counted as crew. Bree was set ashore at the next port, well fed and thoroughly caught, and she thought about those forty buckets for a long time.

The captain's cabin door stood open a crack. Inside, Bree could see a wide table covered in charts, and not a soul in the room. Voices came from the next door along, the one marked OFFICERS, and one of them was dry and quick. It was the voice that had called the order to cast off from the bridge. Captain Quill was in there, and she did not sound pleased. Pip sat down between the two doors and began to wash a paw, as if to say that he would wait.

choices.label: Listen at the officers' door.
Slip into the cabin to see the charts.

nodes.body: Bree put her ear to the officers' door and listened. "He has not eaten since noon, and the glass is falling," said Captain Quill, "so if that storm catches us, he will kick my ship to pieces." A second voice answered, "Then we go around it, Captain, and it costs us a day." A chair scraped. "That is a day more with a crew that thinks it is hauling tea," said the captain. "He hates thunder, and he hates any loud noise at all, so keep that hold quiet, and keep it sealed." Bree's ears prickled with curiosity, because who on earth was HE? Before she could hear more, the whole ship shuddered, and somewhere above, a warning bell began to ring.

choices.label: Back away as the bell rings.

nodes.body: Bree slipped into the cabin with Pip at her heels and bent over the charts, where the top one showed the ship's course as a red line, bending wide around a grey smudge marked STORM. In the corner, somebody had drawn a small whale in pencil, with the word HOME and an arrow pointing east. Why would a captain doodle a whale? Then boots rang in the corridor, coming fast. The chart table was right beside her, but its legs were long and bare. The window curtain hung all the way to the floor, but it was on the far side of the room. The door handle began to turn.

choices.label: Dash for the long curtain.
Dive under the chart table.

nodes.body: Bree reached the long curtain with half a second to spare. Through a gap in the cloth, she watched the first officer stride in, a tall woman with rain on her coat. Pip, in the middle of the floor, had turned into a perfect statue of a cat, and the officer did not even look down. She snatched the storm chart off the table. "Go around it, she says, and lose a whole day, all for the sake of one seasick calf," she muttered. Then the deck jumped under them all, and a bell began to clang. The officer said a word that Bree was not supposed to know, and ran. Bree let out her breath, scooped up the statue, and slipped out after her.

choices.label: Slip out into the corridor.

nodes.body: The corridor pitched hard as the ship met rough air, and the warning bell clanged louder, over and over. Boots pounded across the deck overhead, and doors banged open all along the passage. Bree tucked Pip inside her coat. "Hold on tight," she told him. Nobody had a glance to spare for a girl with a lump in her coat, so she ran after the crew, toward whatever trouble had found the Cirrus.

choices.label: Follow the running crew.

nodes.body: Bree dove under the chart table and pulled in her knees, but it was not enough. The first officer strode in, stopped, and said, "I see two feet, and a tail," and Pip's tail vanished, far too late. She was a tall woman with rain on her coat, and she was trying hard not to smile. "Out you come, both of you," she ordered, and she marched them to the purser, quite gently. But under that table, Bree had seen what nobody was meant to see. Pinned to the underside was a pencil sketch of a small whale with fins like sails, and one word beneath it, NIMBUS. "What is a nimbus?" Bree asked. "It is a kind of cloud," said the officer, a little too quickly. Bree was sent ashore at the next port, still not believing her.

The rope ladder came up into the inner rigging, a warm forest of ropes strung between the decks. Pip scampered ahead as if he had been born up here, while Bree followed more slowly. Before she trusted any rope, she gave it a firm tug, the way careful climbers do. Two ways led onward. One was a catwalk of solid boards with a sturdy rail. The other was a rope-bridge, swaying out toward the great gasbags, with a painted board hanging at its near end. LIVE ROPE, said the board, CROSS LOW AND SLOW. "Mrrp," said Pip from the first plank of the bridge, and he looked back at her.

choices.label: Take the steady catwalk.
Cross the swaying rope-bridge.

nodes.body: The catwalk gave Bree a grand view of the gasbags, which hung overhead like a ceiling of silver moons. Pip trotted along the rail like a tiny rope-dancer. Far above, two riggers were shouting to each other through the ropes. "The glass is dropping, so double-lash the aft bag," called one, and the other called back, "Which seam, the old one, the one that always goes?" Bree looked up, but she could not tell one seam from another. Then the whole ship leaned hard to one side, as the first gust of the storm shoved against the hull. Bree grabbed the rail with both hands.

choices.label: Grip the rail as the ship leans.

nodes.body: Bree stepped out onto the rope-bridge, which swayed like a hammock and sagged low in the middle. The planks were no wider than her two feet together. Pip rode on her shoulder with his claws hooked in her collar. Halfway across, a gust slammed into the ship, and the bridge kicked sideways. The hand ropes went slack, then snapped tight again. The far platform was only six planks away. Behind the wind, Bree heard a second gust coming, bigger than the first.

choices.label: Crouch low and inch across.
Run the last six planks before the gust.

nodes.body: Bree crouched low and slid one knee forward, and then the other. The second gust hit, and the bridge bucked like a pony, but there was not much of Bree left for the wind to push. Low and slow, she told herself, one plank and then another. Pip kept his claws in her collar and his opinions to himself. On the sixth plank, her hand closed around the platform rail. "We did it," she whispered. Somewhere in the ropes above, a rigger who had been watching gave one sharp whistle, the kind that means well done.

choices.label: Climb down from the platform.

nodes.body: The whole rigging shook as the storm took hold of the ship, and the ropes hummed like plucked strings. Far below, a bell clanged without stopping, and voices shouted orders that the wind tore in half. Bree tucked Pip inside her coat. "Hold on tight," she told him. Then she found a ladder and climbed down toward the noise, checking every rung with her foot before she trusted it.

choices.label: Climb down toward the shouting.

nodes.body: Bree ran the last planks, and she made three of them before the gust did. The bridge flipped over like a skipping rope, and when it stopped, she was hanging in the hand ropes with one leg through the netting, as stuck as a fly in a web. She was not falling, but she was not going anywhere at all. Pip sat on the plank above her and calmly washed a paw. A wiry rigger swung across on his own line and looked her over. "Did you read my sign?" he asked. "Low and slow, it says, because ropes do not like to be rushed." He untangled her kindly enough, but he kept her clipped to his belt for the rest of the flight. From his perch, Bree watched black clouds pile up ahead and heard him mutter about an old seam near the stern. At the next port she was handed down to the ground, with a pattern of little rope squares still printed on her leg.

Rain hit the big windows of the main deck like thrown gravel, and the Cirrus pitched until everything not tied down slid to one side. "All hands to the lines, all hands!" roared the bosun, an enormous man with a voice like a foghorn. Sailors ran past Bree without a glance, because tonight a stowaway was only one more pair of legs in a hurry. Out on the weather deck, a loose line cracked like a whip. Near the mast, the crew hauled on a rope and shouted for help. And from far below, in the deep hold, came a long groan that did not sound like timber at all. Inside Bree's coat, Pip's ears turned toward it.

choices.label: Fight through the wind to the weather deck.
Join the crew hauling on the rope.
Go down toward the groan in the deep hold.

nodes.body: The weather deck was a roar of wind and stinging rain, and Bree had to lean into it just to stand. A control line had torn loose near the rail, and it lashed back and forth like an angry snake. A soaked officer clung to the wheelhouse steps. "Belay that line, somebody, before it takes the rail off," he shouted, but nobody else was near enough to hear. The line cracked again. A brass rail post stood within Bree's reach, as solid as a tree. The deck tilted, and her boots began to slide.

choices.label: Crawl low to catch the loose line.
Grab the rail post and hold on.

nodes.body: Bree crawled low across the wet boards and caught the line on its next swing, though it nearly pulled her arm off. She looped it around a cleat in a figure of eight, the way the sailors did in every book she had ever read, and it held. The soaked officer stared at her. "Well caught, but whose girl are you?" he called. Bree opened her mouth, but he had no time for the answer. "Never mind that now, just get below, through that hatch," he said, "and if you pass the deep hold, find out what in thunder is groaning down there."

choices.label: Drop through the hatch.

nodes.body: Bree grabbed the rail post and hugged it with both arms, and for three breaths, that was enough. Then a loose crate came skidding down the tilted deck, straight toward her post. There was a hatch two steps to her left, with its cover banging open and shut. Far across the deck, the wheelhouse door glowed yellow, and everybody who gave the orders was behind it. The crate hit a ring bolt, spun around, and kept coming.

choices.label: Drop down the hatch.
Dash across the open deck to the wheelhouse.

nodes.body: Below decks, the howl of the wind sank to a groan. It was the same groan Bree had heard before, only worse, and it rose and fell like breathing. She followed it down one ladder and then another, to the bottom of the ship. A great door stood there, with a board nailed across it that said SEALED BY ORDER OF THE CAPTAIN. But the storm had shaken the bolt loose, and the door hung open, just wide enough for one thin girl.

choices.label: Slip through the gap in the door.

nodes.body: Bree dashed for the wheelhouse, and she made it about four steps. Then the wind picked her up like a leaf, and a rigger caught her by the collar in midair. "Not tonight, small one," he shouted, and he bundled her below to a safe cabin, cat and all, and wedged the door. She was warm there, and quite unhurt. But all night long, a low, sad note came up through the floor, rising when the thunder cracked and sinking when the thunder passed. Pip sat with his ears pointed at the boards the whole time. By morning the storm had blown itself out, and so had the sound, and nobody would tell Bree what it had been. She rode on to port wrapped in a blanket, sure of only one thing: the hatch had been two steps away, and the answer had been under it.

The crew heaved on a thick rope, with their boots sliding on the wet deck. The rope ran up to the great balloon, and the balloon wanted to get away. "Heave, and heave again, and somebody find me one more pair of hands, because I will take a monkey's!" roared the bosun. The end of the rope trailed free behind the last sailor. A little farther off, a row of red sand-buckets hung on their hooks. "And I want sand on this deck," the bosun bellowed, "before somebody slides clean off my ship."

choices.label: Grab the end of the rope and pull.
Run for the sand-buckets.

nodes.body: Bree grabbed the end of the rope and threw her whole weight on it. It did not feel like much, but a rope did not care who was pulling, only how many. "Heave," roared the bosun, and the line crept backward by one hand, and then by another, until a sailor whipped it around a cleat and it held. The crew let out a hoarse cheer. Somebody thumped Bree on the back so hard that Pip squeaked inside her coat.

choices.label: Catch her breath beside the bosun.

nodes.body: Bree ran for the sand-buckets and unhooked two of them, which were far heavier than they looked. She got them halfway back, one in each hand, leaning like a pair of scales. Then the ship heaved, and the left bucket began to tip, with sand hissing over its rim. The crew were ten steps away, slipping and shouting. The deck tilted further, and both buckets dragged at her arms.

choices.label: Hug the tipping bucket and keep going.
Let the buckets go and grab the rail.

nodes.body: For one breath, the rope was made fast, the deck was sanded, and nobody was shouting. The bosun wiped the rain from his eyes and looked down at Bree, properly, for the first time. "Hold hard," he rumbled. "I know every hand on this ship, down to the cabin boy's freckles, and I do not know you, so who are you, small fry?" Stowaways went to the purser, and everybody knew that. The purser had an office with a lock on the door. But the bosun's face was not unkind, and the ladder to the lower decks was right behind her.

choices.label: Tell the bosun the truth.
Duck away down the ladder.

nodes.body: "I am a stowaway," Bree told the bosun, and it came out very small. The bosun stared at her, and then he laughed like a foghorn with the hiccups. "A stowaway, who works for my crew in the middle of a storm!" He bent down until his beard dripped on her boots. "Then I never heard you say it, small fry, not until this blow is done." A long groan rolled up from the bottom of the ship, and his grin faded. "That is the sealed hold, where nobody goes, by order of the captain," he said, "but nobody ever said a small someone could not look, so go and see, and come and tell me." Bree climbed down three ladders to a great door marked SEALED, where the storm had shaken the bolt loose.

choices.label: Slip through the door of the sealed hold.

nodes.body: Bree ducked under the bosun's arm and ran for the ladder. "Oi, small fry, I was not done asking!" he bellowed, but the ship rolled, a rope groaned, and he had forty other things to shout at. Bree slid down the ladder with her name still safely her own. A long groan rolled up to meet her from the bottom of the ship, and it did not sound like timber. Pip wriggled in her coat and pointed his nose straight down. So Bree kept going, down three ladders, to a great door. A board nailed across it said SEALED BY ORDER OF THE CAPTAIN, but the storm had shaken the bolt loose.

choices.label: Squeeze past the loose bolt.

nodes.body: Bree let the buckets go and grabbed for the rail, but the buckets did not go far. They slid, turned, and came back at her like two red bowling pins, and they knocked her clean off her feet. A hand the size of a shovel caught her before she slid any farther. "Easy, small fry," said the bosun, and he sat her on a coil of rope, out of the way, with Pip in her lap. "You stay put, and that is an order, whoever you are." So she stayed put and watched the crew win their fight without her. Twice, a long groan rolled up from below, and twice the bosun frowned at the hatch to the lower decks. "That is the sealed hold, and I would give my whistle to know what is in it," he muttered. Bree would have given a good deal more. The Cirrus carried them both to port, still wondering.

The deep hold was where the groan was loudest, and it was not the sound of timber creaking. It was the sound of something alive down there, and something afraid. A great door blocked the way, with a board nailed across it that said SEALED BY ORDER OF THE CAPTAIN. Set into the door was a small round hatch with a glass pane, no bigger than a dinner plate. On the wall beside it hung a brass panel, covered in neat handwriting. Pip jumped down from Bree's coat and put both front paws against the door.

choices.label: Peer through the little glass hatch.
Read the brass panel.

nodes.body: Bree wiped the glass with her sleeve and peered through the hatch. Beyond it lay an enormous, dim room, and in the room lay something as pale as a bank of cloud and longer than a lifeboat, and it was shaking. Pip stood up on his hind legs and put his nose to the glass. "Mrrp," he said, as if he were asking a question. The great pale shape went still, and then it answered, with one long low note that shivered through the door and up Bree's arms. Pip looked up at Bree as if to say, well, open it.

choices.label: Lean on the great door.

nodes.body: Bree read the brass panel from top to bottom. It was written in a quick, neat hand, and it was not about cargo at all. FEEDING, it said, forty buckets of mash, morning and night. TENDING, check the harness straps twice a day. CALMING, speak low and move slow, and NEVER shout, and NEVER bang. At the bottom was a signature with a long, curly tail, which belonged to Captain Quill. This was not a storeroom door, then, but the door to somebody's bedroom, and that somebody was groaning.

choices.label: Try the great door.

nodes.body: Thunder boomed, and the whole ship jolted so hard that a bolt jumped out of its bracket. The great door swung open by itself, just wide enough for one thin girl, and warm air breathed out of the dark, smelling of salt and straw. Pip went in first, with his tail straight up like a flag. Bree took one long breath and followed him inside.

choices.label: Step into the dim hold.

nodes.body: Inside lay a sky-whale. He was only a calf, but he filled the hold from wall to wall, cloud-grey, with fins like folded sails and one eye as big as a dinner plate. A card was pinned beside the door in neat, quick writing: NIMBUS, sky-whale calf, cut from a hunter's net, bound for the haven, TELL NO ONE. So this was Nimbus, the captain's secret. Thunder cracked, and Nimbus flinched so hard that his tail struck the hull and the whole ship rolled. Then Pip gave one small mew, and the great eye turned to find him. For a moment Nimbus held perfectly still. "Hoooom," he sang, low and shaky, and the ship steadied. Then the thunder came again, and far above, the crew on the bridge went on fighting a storm they only half understood.

choices.label: Stay and try to calm Nimbus.
Let Pip go to him.
Race to the bridge with the news.
Run to fetch help from the crew.

nodes.body: Bree stayed with Nimbus. She edged closer, one slow step at a time, with Pip trotting ahead as if whales were nothing special. "Easy, now, easy, big one," she said. Up close, she saw what else was wrong. A leather harness was buckled around his middle, and one strap had twisted tight around his left fin, pinning it flat. Every time he tried to move the fin, he jerked, and every jerk rocked the ship. He was watching her with that enormous, wet eye, and he was shaking all over.

choices.label: Hum to Nimbus, soft and low.
Untangle the strap from his fin.

nodes.body: Bree hummed to Nimbus, soft and low. She did not know any whale songs, so she made one up, three notes going down like steps on a ladder. The great eye fixed on her, and the shaking slowed. Then, to her astonishment, Nimbus hummed the three notes back, so deep that her teeth buzzed. "That is it," Bree whispered, "that is our song." The ship stopped rolling quite so hard, and although the strap was still twisted around his fin, he was too busy singing to fight it.

choices.label: Head for the bridge with a plan.

nodes.body: Bree reached up and worked at the strap around his fin, where the leather was wet and stubborn. "Hold still, because I know it pinches," she told Nimbus. Her fingers found the twist, and then the buckle, and the strap slid free. The fin unfolded like a sail in a fair wind, wider than Bree was tall. Nimbus shuddered from nose to tail and breathed out a long, grateful hoooom. He stopped jerking, and the ship stopped lurching quite so hard. Then he laid the free fin on the floor beside her, as gently as a dog lays down a paw.

choices.label: Hurry up to the bridge.

nodes.body: Bree let Pip go. He trotted straight up to the sky-whale, a grey speck beside a grey cloud, round with sardines and afraid of nothing. He sniffed the enormous nose, turned around twice, and lay down against it. Then he began to purr, that rusty, rumbling purr like a tiny engine. Nimbus went perfectly still, and the great eye closed halfway. "Hoooom," he sang, and this time it did not shake. The ship stopped rolling, as if someone had laid a hand on it. Bree stared, because a cat no bigger than a loaf of bread had just done what a whole crew could not.

choices.label: Carry Pip up to the bridge.

nodes.body: Nimbus was calmer now, but the storm was not, and one more crack of thunder would set him thrashing again. Bree knew one thing that nobody on the bridge knew: he steadied when someone small stayed close and stayed gentle. "I will be back, I promise," she told him. She scooped Pip into her coat and climbed, ladder after ladder, to the wheelhouse door, and she did not stop to knock. "Captain, I have been with your whale," she said, "and I know what helps him."

choices.label: Step into the wheelhouse.

nodes.body: Bree tucked Pip into her coat and raced for the bridge with her news, but she got only as far as the main stair. The storm had jammed its door shut, and no amount of shoving would move it. That left two ways up. A long stair wound around the outside of the hull, dry and solid, with a hundred steps at least. A short service passage cut straight through the middle of the ship, but it was already ankle-deep in rainwater, and more was pouring in through a broken vent. Pip peered out at the water and flattened his ears.

choices.label: Take the long, dry stair.
Wade through the short, flooded passage.

nodes.body: The long stair was slow, but it was dry and solid under her boots, and Bree took it two steps at a time. Pip rode in her coat with his chin on her collar and said nothing, which for Pip was high praise. She practiced her speech as she climbed. "Captain, there is a whale in your hold," she tried, but that sounded like a joke. "Captain, your whale is scared of the thunder, and that is what is rocking your ship," she tried next, and that was the one. She said it again on every landing, so that the wind could not steal it.

choices.label: Keep climbing toward the bridge.

nodes.body: Near the top, the stair opened onto the officers' corridor, which was loud with shouted orders and the boom of the storm. A mate with a lantern blocked the way. "Oi, no passengers on this deck!" he said. "I am not a passenger," said Bree, which was perfectly true. She ducked under his lantern before he could work that out. The wheelhouse door stood just ahead, with yellow light leaking around its edges.

choices.label: Push on to the wheelhouse door.

nodes.body: Bree reached the wheelhouse door just as the ship shuddered again, and the glass rattled in its frame. Inside, a dry, quick voice was calling for anything at all that might steady the ship. Bree pushed the door open. "Captain, your whale is scared of the thunder," she said, "and that is what is rocking your ship." It came out exactly as she had practiced it. Every head in the wheelhouse turned.

choices.label: Face the captain.

nodes.body: Bree waded into the flooded passage. The water was at her ankles, then at her knees, and it was cold enough to make her gasp. Pip climbed onto her head and stayed there. Halfway along, the water reached her belt and the lamps went out, and that settled it. She splashed back to the dry end, dripping and shivering, and took the long stair after all. By the time she reached the bridge, the crew had wrestled the ship level the hard way, and it had cost them half the night. Captain Quill herself brought the blanket and sat Bree by the stove, with Pip steaming on her knee. "You saw him, then," she said quietly. "A slow messenger still arrives, Stowaway, but a wet one mostly sneezes." Bree sneezed. She rode on to port warm and dry, with a secret she had carried all that way and never got to use.

Bree tucked Pip into her coat and ran to fetch help, because this was too big for one girl and one cat. But who would listen to a stowaway? The bosun had the loudest voice on the ship, and half the crew jumped whenever he coughed. The captain knew what was truly in that hold. Bree burst out onto the main deck. To her left, the bosun stood roaring at the mast, and straight ahead, a tall figure in a captain's coat stood alone at a rain-streaked window.

choices.label: Run to the bosun.
Run to the bosun.
Go straight to the captain.

nodes.body: Bree ran to the bosun and pulled his sleeve. "Small fry, what did you find down there?" he asked, and she told him everything in one breath, the whale and the card and the thunder. His eyes went as round as portholes. A man who did not know her would have laughed, but this girl had told him she was a stowaway when a fib would have served her better. "A whale in my hold, and the captain knew about it," he said slowly, shaking himself like a wet dog. "Right, then, she will want to hear this from you, so stay close behind me." He charged up the ladder ahead of her, bellowing for the captain to come and hear what the small fry had found in her hold.

choices.label: Follow the bosun to the wheelhouse.

nodes.body: Bree ran to the bosun and pulled his sleeve, and he looked down at her the way a mountain looks at a goat. "A whale in my hold," he repeated, when she had gasped it all out, "says a girl I do not know from a hole in the deck." He did not believe one word of it, but he did not let go of her, either. Instead he tucked her under one arm like a rolled-up sail. "Tall tales and strange girls both go to the captain," he said. Then he carried her up the ladder, bellowing for the captain to come and hear this one. Pip peered out of Bree's coat like a very small lookout.

choices.label: Ride up to the wheelhouse under his arm.

nodes.body: Bree went straight to the captain, who stood braced at the window, watching the storm with tired eyes. "I have seen Nimbus," Bree said, because it was all she could think of. Captain Quill turned around very slowly. "Have you, indeed," she said, "and how did a girl with a cat in her coat get past my sealed door?" Bree lifted her chin and answered, "The storm shook it open, and I went in." For a moment the captain said nothing, and then one corner of her mouth went up. "Then walk with me, Stowaway, and talk fast, because I have a ship to save and no time to be surprised."

choices.label: Walk with the captain to the wheel.

nodes.body: The wheelhouse doors banged open in a gust of rain. Bree came through them with Pip, and the wind slammed them shut behind her. Inside, lamps swung and charts slid across the floor, while the helmsman fought the wheel with both arms. Nobody asked what a girl was doing on the bridge, because there was no time.

choices.label: Cross the wheelhouse to the wheel.

nodes.body: The Cirrus dropped like a stone, and the lamps swung wildly. "We are losing height, Captain," cried the helmsman. Captain Quill gripped the rail beside the wheel. "I know what is rocking us," she said, "because he is frightened, he is strong, and he is right under our feet." She pulled the brass cap off a speaking tube and added, "This runs straight down to his hold." A rigger burst in, soaked to the skin, shouting that the envelope was tearing aft. From the door, the bosun rumbled, "And the crew have no idea what they are fighting." Far below, Nimbus boomed, and a cargo door banged in the wind. The captain looked at Bree. "You have been nearer to him tonight than any of us, Stowaway, so tell me where you want to stand."

choices.label: Take the speaking tube and steady Nimbus.
Go with the rigger to the torn envelope.
Go below to move Nimbus somewhere safer.
Tell the crew the captain's secret.

nodes.body: Bree took hold of the speaking tube, which was cold brass, as wide as her fist, and smelled of rain. "He will hear whatever goes into that," said Captain Quill, "and I need him still for ten minutes, Stowaway, only ten, and then we can climb out of this." Thunder cracked right over the ship. Far down the tube, Nimbus boomed in fright, and the deck lurched under their feet. The storm was so loud, and the hold was so far away. Bree put her mouth to the brass, and inside her coat, Pip shifted and stretched.

choices.label: Hum into the tube, low and slow.
Call down the tube, loud enough to beat the storm.
Hold Pip up to the tube.

nodes.body: Bree hummed into the tube, low and slow. She kept it soft, three notes going down like steps, over and over again. For a long moment nothing came back but the storm, and then the brass buzzed against her lips with a deep, familiar hoooom. Nimbus was answering her. He was growing still, bit by bit, and as he stilled, the ship stopped fighting itself. "She answers the helm, Captain," cried the helmsman. "Do not stop, Stowaway," said Captain Quill, "whatever happens, do not stop."

choices.label: Keep humming through the worst of it.

nodes.body: Bree did not stop. She hummed until her lips went numb and her voice went scratchy. Whenever the thunder cracked, she hummed a little lower, and whenever Nimbus wavered, she hummed a little slower. The crew held their course by the sound of it. Minute by minute, the pitching eased into a gentle sway. Then the rain thinned, the clouds tore open, and the Cirrus rose into calm air, with a round white moon waiting above.

choices.label: Ride out into the moonlit sky.

nodes.body: Bree called down the tube as loudly as she could. "NIMBUS, IT IS ALL RIGHT!" she shouted, and the brass tube swallowed her voice and made it enormous. Down in the hold, it came out like one more crack of thunder, and Nimbus thrashed until the Cirrus rolled so far that the charts slid off the table. "Cap it," cried the captain, slamming the cover on the tube herself. After that, the crew had to fight the storm the hard way, all night long, and they won, but only just. At the next port, Captain Quill walked Bree down the tower herself. "He has never liked a raised voice, not the thunder's and not mine," she said. "It was a brave try, Stowaway, and a loud one." Bree looked back at the ship. Somewhere inside it, a whale was still waiting for somebody to sing to him softly.

The Cirrus sailed on through clean, quiet night air. Captain Quill took the speaking tube from Bree's stiff fingers and capped it herself, and then, in front of the whole crew, she shook Bree's hand. "I asked you for ten minutes, and you gave me forty," she said. "That is not a stowaway, that is one of the ship's own." Far below, a sleepy hoooom drifted up the tube, and the helmsman laughed out loud. Three days later, Nimbus swam out into the haven, safe among his own kind. Bree watched from the rail, with Pip purring on her shoulder and the whole sky ahead.

Bree lifted Pip out of her coat and held him up to the tube. "A cat," said Captain Quill, "your whole plan is a cat." "He is full of sardines, and he purrs when he is full," said Bree. She scratched him under the chin, and Pip closed his eyes. The purr started, rusty and rumbling, and the brass tube swallowed it and made it enormous. It rolled down through the ship like a tiny engine the size of a house. Far below, the booming stopped, and then, up the tube, soft and steady, came the answering hoooom.

choices.label: Keep Pip purring.

nodes.body: Pip purred for a solid hour. Bree's arms ached from holding him, so the helmsman held him, and then the bosun, and Pip purred for all of them like a cat who had always known his own worth. Down in the hold, Nimbus slept. The Cirrus climbed out of the storm as smooth as cream. "Thirty years in the sky," said Captain Quill, "and I have never once been rescued by a cat." She had it written in the ship's log exactly that way. Pip was made ship's cat, with a sardine ration for life. Bree was made his keeper, which meant she had to stay aboard, and nobody could think of a single reason why not.

ending.title: The Purr Heard Round the Ship

nodes.body: Bree went with the rigger, up through the inner rigging to the roaring dark under the envelope. High above them, a long tear had opened along one seam, and the gasbag behind it bulged through like a tongue. "I cannot fit past those ribs, but somebody small could," shouted the rigger, a wiry man with a coil of patch-line on his shoulder. He looked hard at Bree. "Have you ever crossed live rope? I do not mean a catwalk, I mean rope that moves under you." Beside him stood a big iron winch that pulled the patch tight from below, with a handle as long as Bree's arm.

choices.label: Climb the rigging to the tear.
Climb the rigging to the tear.
Work the winch from below.

nodes.body: Bree looked up at the tear and nodded. "I crossed one tonight, a rope-bridge, in the first gust of the storm," she said. The rigger's eyebrows climbed toward his cap. "So that was you, the small someone I saw crossing my bridge, low and slow," he said, clipping a safety line to her belt and tugging it twice. "Then up you go, exactly the same way." Bree climbed, and whenever the ropes bucked, she let them buck. She squeezed between the ribs where no grown rigger could fit, and threaded the patch-line through, hole by hole. "Haul away," she called, and far below, the line went tight, and the long tear closed like a mouth.

choices.label: Watch the mended envelope hold.

nodes.body: Bree threw herself on the winch, and the handle fought her like a live thing. She cranked it round with all her weight, again and again, until her arms burned. High above, the rigger had found a ship's boy thin enough to reach the tear, and he shouted down for her to haul. Bree hauled, and click by click, the patch-line drew tight, the gasbag slid back behind its seam, and the long tear closed. The floor stopped dropping away beneath her boots.

choices.label: Hold the winch until the ship steadies.

nodes.body: The patch held, and the Cirrus stopped sinking, shook herself, and climbed into a sky full of stars. Down in the hold, with the ship flying level at last, Nimbus settled and slept. The riggers swore up and down that the small one had saved them all. "She crossed my bridge in a gust and climbed my rigging in a storm, and all on her first night," said the wiry rigger. Captain Quill heard the whole story and then asked to hear it again. She signed Bree on as rigger's mate, the youngest the Cirrus had ever carried. Pip signed on too, by walking across the wet ink of the ship's log.

Steady lift won the night, and the Cirrus righted herself over a calming sea of cloud. When the rigger climbed down, he found Bree still hanging on the winch handle, too tired to let go. The crew lifted her onto their shoulders, and Captain Quill laughed for the first time that long night. "Any sailor who can work a winch like that has a berth on my ship whenever she likes," she said. Then she lowered her voice so that only Bree could hear. "My cargo sleeps sounder on a level ship, and he thanks you too." Bree fell asleep in a hammock that night with Pip on her feet, and the engines hummed her all the way to morning.

Bree had never crossed live rope in her life, but she climbed into the rigging toward the tear anyway, because somebody had to. She got ten ropes up before the ship rolled, and every rope she was holding moved a different way at once. Her arms locked, and then her legs locked. She stuck to the rigging like a burr on a sock, and she could not go up or down. Pip climbed up and sat on her head, which did not help. The rigger had to leave the tear and fetch her, and those were minutes the Cirrus did not have. The ship limped down to an emergency mooring with her envelope flapping. "Nobody is born knowing ropes," the rigger told her, quite gently. "They are learned in calm air, and there is a whole forest of them inside this ship, with catwalks and a rope-bridge and all." Bree stood on the mooring tower and looked up at the sagging balloon. A rope-bridge had been there all night, waiting to teach her, and she had gone another way.

Bree went below with the captain, back to Nimbus, who was bumping the hull again so that each bump shook the lamps. "He is not only frightened," said Captain Quill. "He is big enough to fly, he knows it, and he wants out." At the far end of the hold, the storm had torn the great cargo door half open. Rain blew through the gap, and beyond it lay nothing but dark, racing sky. "If he goes, he goes as he is, because I have not been able to get near that harness since the first thunder," the captain added. On the other side of the hold, a smaller door led to the inner bay, padded and windowless and still.

choices.label: Open the cargo door and let Nimbus fly.
Open the cargo door and let Nimbus fly.
Coax Nimbus into the quiet inner bay.

nodes.body: Bree put her shoulder to the cargo door, and the captain pushed beside her. "His fin is free, because I untangled the strap myself," Bree panted. Captain Quill gave her a long look, said, "Did you, now," and slipped the last buckle of the harness so that it fell away. Nimbus turned his great head toward the gap and gathered himself. For one long moment he did not move at all. "Go on," Bree whispered, "it is your sky." He slid out into the storm, and he did not fall, but opened both fins like sails and rose.

choices.label: Watch Nimbus take to the air.

nodes.body: Nimbus swam through the storm as if it were calm water, and wherever he flew, the wind seemed to go gentle around him. He circled the Cirrus once, and his long low song rolled over the decks. Every sailor aboard stopped to stare. "What in thunder is THAT?" roared the bosun. "That," said Captain Quill, "is why we fly east." Then Nimbus turned and swam ahead of the ship, and the helmsman followed his pale shape through a gap in the clouds that no chart had ever shown.

choices.label: Follow Nimbus toward the haven.

nodes.body: Nimbus led the Cirrus out of the storm and all the way to the haven. At dawn, the crew lined the rail to watch as a dozen grey shapes rose from the clouds below to meet him, singing. He circled the ship one last time, so close that Bree could have touched his fin. "Hoooom," he sang, and it did not shake at all, and then he was gone among his own kind. Captain Quill stood beside Bree for a long while. "He flew straight because somebody took the time to free that fin," she said, "and you have a berth on my ship for as long as you want one." "Mrrp," said Pip, which settled the matter.

Bree coaxed Nimbus toward the inner bay, one slow step at a time. She walked backward in front of his nose, humming, and he followed the hum like a very large duckling. "A storm is no place for a first flight," said the captain, padding the walls with spare canvas. Inside the bay there was no window, no thunder, and no wind. Nimbus sank down with a long sigh that fluttered Bree's hair, and the thrashing stopped. Up on the bridge, the helmsman felt the ship come back into his hands.

choices.label: Settle Nimbus for the voyage.

nodes.body: Snug in his padded bay, Nimbus rode out the storm, and Bree stayed with him the whole night. When the thunder came, she hummed, and when it passed, she told him about the sky outside. Three days later, the Cirrus reached the haven, where the keepers could not get over it. "A calf this calm, after a storm like that," they said, "and who was it that sat with him?" Captain Quill pointed at Bree. Best of all, Bree got to stand on the cargo ramp when Nimbus swam out to join his own kind. He looked back once and sang one last hoooom, and then he was a grey shape among other grey shapes, and Bree waved until her arm was tired.

Bree and the captain heaved the cargo door open, and Nimbus threw himself at the sky. He got one fin out. The other was pinned flat against his side by a twisted strap of his harness, and no whale could fly on one fin. He did not fall, but hung there, bobbing behind the ship on the end of his own harness line, like the biggest kite in the world. He seemed to rather like it. He stopped thrashing, and the Cirrus stopped rolling, and that was how they flew out of the storm: one airship, towing one whale. "Thirty years in the sky," said Captain Quill, "and I arrive at port flying a kite." Every child in the harbor town cheered. But Nimbus could not swim on to the haven that way, and the keepers had to rest his sore fin for a week first. "One twisted strap," the captain sighed. "If only somebody had got close enough to free it before that door opened."

"The crew should know," said Bree, and the wheelhouse went quiet. Captain Quill's eyes were grey and very steady. "That secret has kept him alive," she said, "because hunters pay well for a sky-whale, and sailors talk in port." "They are fighting a storm they cannot see," said Bree. Her voice wobbled, but she got it all out. "They cannot help him if they do not know he is there." The bosun shifted his great boots in the doorway. Behind him, wet faces crowded the ladder, waiting for orders. Far below, Nimbus boomed again, and the faces on the ladder looked at one another.

choices.label: Tell the crew herself, right now.

Lead the crew down to see Nimbus.

nodes.body: Bree told the crew herself, standing on a chart locker so that they could all see her. "There is a sky-whale calf in the sealed hold, he is scared of the thunder, and that is what is throwing the ship about," she said. Somebody laughed, but the bosun's voice rolled over the laugh like a wave. "This one told me to my face that she was a stowaway, when a fib would have served her better, so if she says whale, it is a whale," he roared. "Port watch to the hold, and step softly, and starboard watch with me!" Nobody laughed after that. Everybody ran.

choices.label: Run with the port watch.

nodes.body: The port watch sat with Nimbus all night, taking turns to hum, while the starboard watch flew the ship. By dawn, the storm was a grey smear behind them, and half the crew had been sung to sleep by a whale. Afterward they hung a hammock for Bree in their own quarters. They stitched her name on a spare jersey, a little crooked. "A girl who works that hard and talks that straight is no stowaway, she is a shipmate," said the bosun. Captain Quill said only, "I should have told them myself, weeks ago." Then she saluted Bree, which the crew talked about for years.

Bree told the crew herself, standing on a chart locker so that they could all see her. "There is a sky-whale calf in the sealed hold, and he is scared of the thunder," she said. There was a short silence, and then the whole ladder roared with laughter. "A whale, in OUR hold, and pull the other one, it has bells on," somebody shouted. The bosun scratched his beard and said, "I do not know this girl, and I never met a whale." Not one of them moved. They were not being unkind, but they had no reason at all to believe a stranger with a cat in her coat. Bree jumped down off the locker.

choices.label: Drag the bosun to the hold.

nodes.body: Bree asked the captain to tell them. "It is your secret, so it should come from you," she said. Captain Quill looked at the crowded ladder for a long moment, and then she told them, in four short sentences, and not one sailor laughed. "Port watch to the hold, and step softly," she finished. Then she turned back to Bree. "He has seen you tonight, and he did not mind you, so I could use you at his side, where it will not be safe or dry. Or there is a warm bunk below, and no shame in taking it, because you have done a night's work already."

choices.label: Take the place at his side.
Take the warm bunk below.

nodes.body: Bree took her place at the side of the sky-whale, between the captain and the port watch. It was not safe, and it was certainly not dry. Each time the thunder cracked, she laid a hand on his nose and hummed, and the captain hummed with her, half a note off. "Do not tell the crew that I sing," said Captain Quill, and the bosun answered, "They already know." By dawn the storm had broken. The captain wrote Bree's name in the ship's log with her own pen, and then, in front of everyone, she read it out. "Bree, who came aboard as a stowaway, and who stays as crew."

Bree took the warm bunk below, and she had not known how tired she was until she saw the blanket. The crew brought the ship through the storm without her, and she did not get to see the end of it. But she had ridden out a real storm on a real sky-ship, and she had looked a sky-whale in the eye. Near dawn, a long, calm note hummed up through the bunk, and Pip purred back at it in his sleep. At port, Captain Quill shook her hand. "Come back when you are taller, and bring the cat," she said. Bree walked down the tower with a story nobody at home would believe, and a very good reason to grow.

Words were too slow. Bree grabbed the bosun's sleeve and pulled, and because she pulled so hard, he came. The rest came after him, grumbling, down three ladders to the sealed hold, where Captain Quill pushed the great door wide herself. Lamplight fell on a cloud-grey calf as long as a lifeboat, shivering from nose to tail. Nobody laughed, and nobody said anything at all. Then the bosun took off his cap. "Well, I will be keelhauled," he whispered, very gently, so as not to frighten him. And the whole crew, still dripping, sat down on the floor of the hold and began, one by one, to hum.

choices.label: Hum with the whole crew.

nodes.body: The whole crew hummed Nimbus through the storm, forty voices, most of them flat, and he did not seem to mind. The officers flew the ship, and the Cirrus came out the far side of the weather at sunrise. The secret was not a secret anymore, but a wonder that belonged to everyone aboard. The cook brought the mash himself. "So THIS is where my forty buckets go," he said, and Nimbus blew a happy gust of fish breath in his face. Captain Quill found Bree at the rail. "I was afraid to trust them, and you were not," she said, "so sail with us, Stowaway." Bree said yes before the captain had finished asking.
